name: Maurice Bishop International Airport
before:
Grenada's international airport, on Point Salines at the south western tip of the island, with the capital St George's about 8 km to the north.

It was built to solve a real problem. The old Pearls Airport on the north side of the island had a short and geographically difficult runway that long-range jets could not use, so tourists faced delays getting to Grenada. Point Salines was designed to replace it.

The airport has a heavy political history. Its construction, partly by Cuban workers, was cited by President Ronald Reagan as evidence that the Grenadian government meant to let it be used as a staging point for Soviet military aircraft bound for Cuba. Prime Minister Maurice Bishop's government maintained it was for European and North American tourists. The airport now carries Bishop's name.

The single runway is 2,744 metres at an elevation of 12 metres.

It was formerly called Point Salines Airport, so both names appear in supplier systems.
after:
Grenada's international airport, at Point Salines in the south west of the island, with the capital St George's about 8 km to the north.

The airport has a heavy political history. Cuban workers helped to build it, and in 1983 President Ronald Reagan said it looked suitable for Soviet military aircraft. Prime Minister Maurice Bishop's government said it was for tourists. The airport now carries Bishop's name.

Its single runway is 2,744 metres, at an elevation of 12 metres.

It was formerly called Point Salines Airport, so both names appear in supplier systems.

claims.note: Reagan's own words from the Reagan Library: in March 1983 'the Cubans ... are in the process of building an airfield', and in October 1983 'several hundred Cubans working on the airport'. Wikipedia says it was built in part by Cuban workers, with Canadian design and European and American contractors, so 'helped to build' rather than 'built'.

claims.claim: in 1983 Reagan said it looked suitable for Soviet military aircraft
claims.inAfter: in 1983 President Ronald Reagan said it looked suitable for Soviet military aircraft
claims.note: Was 'cited by President Ronald Reagan as evidence that the Grenadian government meant to let it be used as a staging point for Soviet military aircraft bound for Cuba'. Reagan's own words (27 October 1983) are that it 'looked suspiciously suitable for military aircraft, including Soviet-built long-range bombers'; in March 1983 he asked 'Who is it intended for?' and called it Soviet-Cuban 'power projection into the region'. Neither speech says 'bound for Cuba', which is Wikipedia's reading, so the text keeps to what both support. The year is the date of both speeches.

claims.wasBefore: It was built to solve a real problem. The old Pearls Airport on the north side of the island had a short and geographically difficult runway that long-range jets could not use, so tourists faced delays getting to Grenada. Point Salines was designed to replace it.
claims.why: Wikipedia alone. The Grenada Airports Authority's site (gaa.gd, from the infobox) answered 502, the Government of Grenada's home page has no airport history, and the US Army's history site refused the link lister (403). OurAirports confirms only that Pearls Airport is closed, and places it in St Andrew parish on the east coast, which sits awkwardly with 'the north side of the island'.

claims.why: Reworded to what Reagan's own speeches and Wikipedia both say: Cuban workers helped build it, Reagan said it looked suitable for Soviet military aircraft, and Bishop's government said it was for tourists (see above). 'Bound for Cuba' and 'European and North American' rest on Wikipedia alone.

The UK CAA's 2025 route table has 37,058 scheduled passengers between Gatwick and Grenada in 2025 (39,518 in 2024) and only 202 between Heathrow and Grenada (634 in 2024). The Grenada Tourism Authority's page still lists British Airways three times a week from Gatwick and Virgin Atlantic twice a week from Heathrow, in a list whose other entries are dated 2023; the CAA's tiny Heathrow figures suggest the Virgin line is out of date. An airline's own page would be needed before any of this goes in.
